title: MERN Stack Development
description: Integrate React, Express, MongoDB, and Node into one cohesive application: structure the project, build a dependable API, wire the client to it, and ship it with authentication and production hardening.
objectives: Trace a request through every layer of the MERN stack
Structure a configurable server and client codebase
Build a validated, paginated REST API with Express and Mongoose
Connect a React client with loading, error, and optimistic states
Add JWT authentication and prepare the app for production

modules.title: MERN Architecture & Project Setup
modules.description: How the four layers fit together, and how to scaffold a clean, configurable project.
modules.completionCriteria: Scaffold a MERN repo where an Express server connects to MongoDB and exposes a health-checked API the React client can reach.

lessons.title: The MERN Request Lifecycle
objectives: Trace a request from React through Express to MongoDB
Assign clear ownership to each layer

content.introduction: MERN is four layers passing data back and forth: React renders and initiates requests, Express routes them, Mongoose maps them to MongoDB, and the result travels back as JSON to update the UI.
content.explanation: A typical flow: a React event handler calls fetch('/api/jobs'), Express matches the path and method, a handler runs a Mongoose query, Mongoose serializes documents into plain objects, and Express sends them with a status code. The contract between the frontend and backend is JSON plus HTTP status codes — nothing else. Keeping that contract explicit is what lets you swap or rewrite either side without breaking the other.

examples.title: An Express handler at the center of the flow
examples.walkthrough: The route reads a param, queries Mongo, and answers with JSON. Errors are delegated to Express so one handler formats them consistently for the client.

content.useCase: Any feature where a user action in React must read or write a MongoDB document.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where does Express sit in the MERN request lifecycle?
options: Between the browser and the database, routing HTTP requests
Inside the browser as a rendering engine
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Express receives HTTP requests from the client and is the only layer that talks to MongoDB through Mongoose.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the data contract between the React client and the Express API?
options: JSON bodies with HTTP status codes
Direct MongoDB connections from the browser
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The client sends and receives JSON; status codes signal success or the kind of failure.

content.summary: React initiates, Express routes, Mongoose queries, JSON returns. Keep the HTTP contract explicit on both sides.

lessons.title: Project Structure and Configuration
objectives: Split server and client into a clear folder layout
Load secrets from environment variables

content.introduction: A MERN app grows fast. A boring, predictable layout plus strict environment configuration prevents the 'works on my machine' class of bugs.
content.explanation: Keep server and client in one repo but in separate folders with their own package.json, so each can build and deploy independently. Centralize configuration in one module that reads process.env and fails fast when a required variable is missing — never scatter process.env calls through handlers. Secrets never belong in code or committed .env files; only non-secret defaults live in the repo.

examples.title: Fail-fast configuration module
examples.walkthrough: One module owns all configuration and crashes at startup if something is missing — the failure surfaces immediately instead of at the first login. Typical layout: server/src/{routes,models,config.js} and client/src/.

content.useCase: Every environment: local dev, staging, and production each supply their own .env values.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should secrets like MONGO_URI live?
options: In environment variables read at startup
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Environment variables keep secrets out of source control and let each environment supply its own values.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why throw at startup when a required variable is missing?
options: It fails fast, before any request is mishandled
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An early crash is cheap and obvious; a missing value discovered mid-request is a production incident.

content.summary: Separate server and client folders, centralize config in one fail-fast module, keep secrets in environment variables.

lessons.title: Mongoose Connection and Models
objectives: Open a resilient Mongoose connection
Model API resources with schemas

content.introduction: Your API is only as trustworthy as its data layer. A single shared connection and well-chosen schemas keep it predictable.
content.explanation: Mongoose connects once at startup and reuses that connection for every query — connecting per request would exhaust the database's connection pool. Schemas do more than type your documents: they enforce shape, set defaults, and can run transforms such as hiding a password hash. Index fields you sort or filter on, because a collection scan on every request will eventually time out.

examples.title: Connection helper and a Job model
examples.walkthrough: connectDB is called once from server entry. The schema marks title as required, enables timestamps, and adds an index for the sort the list endpoint uses.

content.useCase: Any collection your API reads or writes: jobs, users, applications, audit logs.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should the Mongoose connection be opened?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Mongoose pools connections; one startup connection is shared by all queries.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why index a field you frequently sort or filter on?
options: It lets MongoDB find and order rows without scanning the whole collection
It converts the field to JSON
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Indexes give MongoDB a sorted lookup path, turning a full collection scan into a direct read.

content.summary: Connect once at startup, encode invariants in schemas, and index every field you query.

modules.title: Building the API Layer
modules.description: Routes, validation, error handling, and query patterns that make an API dependable.
modules.completionCriteria: Ship a CRUD API with validated request bodies, pagination, and a single centralized error handler.

lessons.title: Resource-Oriented Routes
objectives: Map REST verbs to CRUD operations
Mount feature routers from one entry point

content.introduction: REST APIs are easier to use when URLs name resources and verbs name actions. Express makes that mapping a few lines per resource.
content.explanation: One noun-based path per resource — /api/jobs — with GET for reading, POST for creating, PATCH for partial updates, and DELETE for removing. Express Router gives each resource its own file, which you mount on the app at a prefix. This keeps route files small, makes the URL structure readable at a glance, and lets two developers work on different resources without touching the same file.

examples.title: A jobs router
examples.walkthrough: Each verb maps to one operation. Mounting with a prefix composes the full URL, so the router file never needs to know its own path.

content.useCase: Any multi-resource backend: jobs, applications, users, and reports each get their own router.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which method conventionally creates a new resource?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: POST to /api/jobs creates a job under the collection.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does app.use("/api/jobs", router) do?
options: Mounts the router at that path prefix
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Routes defined as "/" inside the router then match /api/jobs.

content.summary: Noun URLs, verb semantics, one router per resource, mounted from a single entry point.

lessons.title: Validation and Error Handling
objectives: Validate request bodies before handlers run
Centralize error responses

content.introduction: Never trust the client. Validate at the edge of your API and answer every failure the same way.
content.explanation: A validation middleware runs before your handler and rejects malformed input with a 400, so handlers can assume the body is well-formed. For errors, Express distinguishes normal middleware (3 args) from error middleware (4 args): calling next(err) jumps straight to the error handler, which logs once and returns one consistent JSON shape. That means a database failure and a bad request reach the client in the same format, and the client only needs one error path.

examples.title: Validation middleware
examples.walkthrough: The schema checks and normalizes the body once; createJob only ever sees clean data. Registered last, the error middleware catches anything thrown downstream.

content.useCase: Every write endpoint: creating jobs, registering users, submitting applications.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should request validation happen?
options: In middleware before the route handler
In the browser's HTML5 attributes only
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Client-side checks are UX; server-side validation is the actual security boundary.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does Express recognize an error-handling middleware?
options: It takes four arguments: err, req, res, next
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The four-argument signature is what makes next(err) route to it.

content.summary: Validate in middleware, delegate failures with next(err), and answer every error in one consistent shape.

lessons.title: Pagination and Query Building
objectives: Paginate list endpoints
Whitelist query parameters instead of trusting input

content.introduction: List endpoints are where APIs break under load. Bounded pagination and careful query construction keep them fast.
content.explanation: Return a fixed page size with a hard maximum, and always send the total count so clients can render page controls. The critical rule: never pass user input straight into a query. Whitelist the fields a client may filter and sort on, otherwise a crafted ?sort[$ne]=1 can become a MongoDB operator injection. Build the filter from an allowlist of known keys instead.

examples.title: Paginated, allowlisted list endpoint
examples.walkthrough: limit is capped at 50, sort only accepts keys from SORTABLE, and filter is built from fixed values — the client can influence the query but never control its shape.

content.useCase: Job boards, search results, feeds, and admin tables — any list that can grow without bound.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why cap the page size on a list endpoint?
options: To prevent one request from pulling an unbounded amount of data
To force clients to use GraphQL
To make JSON smaller in the browser
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An attacker (or a bug) requesting 100000 rows can exhaust memory and connections.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is MongoDB operator injection?
options: User input interpreted as query operators like $ne
knowledgeCheck.explanation: If raw input becomes part of the query object, a client can smuggle in operators; allowlisting prevents it.

content.summary: Bound every list with pagination, allowlist filter and sort keys, and return counts alongside items.

modules.title: Connecting Frontend and Backend
modules.description: Wire React to the API: one shared client, mutations, and optimistic UI.
modules.completionCriteria: Build a React feature that performs full CRUD against the API with correct loading, error, and rollback behavior.

lessons.title: A Shared API Client in React
objectives: Wrap fetch in one reusable client
Surface loading and error states

content.introduction: Scattering raw fetch calls through components produces duplicated parsing, inconsistent errors, and forgotten status checks. One small client fixes all three.
content.explanation: A shared api() helper prefixes the base path, sets headers, checks res.ok, and throws a typed Error carrying the server's message. Components then handle exactly two outcomes — data or a thrown error — which maps cleanly onto loading and error UI. Centralizing this is also where you later attach an auth token and handle a 401 redirect in exactly one place.

examples.title: The api() helper
examples.walkthrough: One place parses errors, one place serializes bodies, one place handles 204s. Components call api() and treat a thrown error as the failure path.

content.useCase: Every data operation in the app: lists, detail views, forms, and deletes.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why check res.ok instead of relying on try/catch alone?
options: fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx responses
try/catch cannot be used with async
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A 404 or 500 resolves normally; only a network failure rejects. You must inspect the status yourself.

knowledgeCheck.question: What benefit does a single api() helper provide?
options: It removes the need for a backend
Headers, error parsing, and auth tokens are handled in one place
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cross-cutting concerns change once, in one file, for the whole app.

content.summary: One fetch wrapper owns headers, serialization, and errors; components only handle data or a thrown error.

lessons.title: Mutations and List Refresh
objectives: Send POST/PATCH/DELETE with JSON bodies
Update derived state after a mutation

content.introduction: Reading data is only half the story. Writes must update the server, then bring the UI back in sync.
content.explanation: A mutation posts a JSON body to your API and then refreshes whatever the server owns. Two details matter: disable the submit button while a request is in flight so a double-click cannot create duplicate records, and reset the form only after success so the user's input survives a failure. After the server confirms, either append the returned document to your list or refetch the list — the server response, not the client draft, is the source of truth.

examples.title: Create form with in-flight protection
examples.walkthrough: saving prevents duplicate submissions, the form clears only on success, and the server's response — not the local draft — is what enters the list.

content.useCase: Creating a job, editing a profile, submitting an application — any form that writes to MongoDB.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why disable the submit button while a mutation is in flight?
options: To make the UI look polished
To prevent duplicate submissions from double-clicks
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Two rapid clicks can otherwise create two records.

knowledgeCheck.question: After a successful create, what should enter the list?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The server owns ids, timestamps, and defaults — only its response is authoritative.

content.summary: Guard against double submits, keep input on failure, and trust the server's response over the local draft.

lessons.title: Optimistic Updates and Rollbacks
objectives: Apply optimistic updates
Roll back state when the server rejects the change

content.introduction: Waiting for the server before rendering makes every click feel slow. Optimistic updates paint the expected result immediately — and require a rollback plan.
content.explanation: The pattern: apply the change to local state, fire the request, and if it fails restore the previous state and surface the error. The important discipline is capturing a snapshot before you mutate, because after the change you can no longer reconstruct what was there. Use optimism for idempotent, low-risk actions like toggles and deletes; skip it when the server must compute the result — a checkout total or a uniqueness check cannot be guessed.

examples.title: Delete with snapshot rollback
examples.walkthrough: The row disappears instantly; on a failed delete it reappears exactly as it was, because the pre-change array was captured up front.

content.useCase: Star toggles, dismissible notifications, list removals, and status chips.

knowledgeCheck.question: What must you capture before applying an optimistic update?
options: The previous state, so it can be restored on failure
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Once local state is mutated, the old value is gone unless you snapshot it.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should you avoid optimistic updates?
options: When the server must compute or validate the result
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Guessing a result the server must decide — pricing, uniqueness — leads to visible wrong states.

content.summary: Paint first, confirm after, roll back from a snapshot on failure — and skip optimism when the server decides the outcome.

modules.title: Auth, Deployment & Production Readiness
modules.description: Authentication, route protection, and the hardening needed before you go live.
modules.completionCriteria: Protect API routes with JWT middleware, handle 401s in the client, and deploy with baseline security and a health check.

lessons.title: Session-Based Auth with JWT
objectives: Hash passwords and verify them safely
Issue and validate signed tokens

content.introduction: Authentication proves who a request belongs to. With stateless JWTs, the server signs a token at login and trusts it later without storing sessions.
content.explanation: Passwords are never stored directly — a bcrypt hash with a per-user salt makes each hash unique even for identical passwords, and verification runs the hash algorithm against the candidate. On successful login the server signs a small JSON payload (subject id, role) with a secret and an expiry. Because verification only needs the secret, no session table is required; the tradeoff is that tokens stay valid until expiry, so keep the lifetime short and plan for revocation.

examples.title: Login endpoint that issues a token
examples.walkthrough: Both a missing user and a wrong password return the same 401 so attackers cannot probe which emails exist. The token carries only an id and role — never the password hash.

content.useCase: Any app with accounts: job boards where applicants and employers have different identities.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why store a bcrypt hash instead of the plain password?
options: A database leak does not reveal usable passwords
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Bcrypt is deliberately slow and salted, so even a stolen table is impractical to crack quickly.

knowledgeCheck.question: Should a login response reveal whether the email exists?
options: No — return the same error for unknown email and wrong password
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Distinct errors let attackers enumerate valid accounts.

content.summary: Hash with bcrypt, sign short-lived tokens with a server secret, and answer login failures uniformly.

lessons.title: Protecting the API and the Client
objectives: Guard routes with auth middleware
Handle 401s in the React client

content.introduction: A token is only useful if something checks it. Auth middleware turns a header into a trusted request identity.
content.explanation: requireAuth reads the Authorization: Bearer header, verifies the signature and expiry, and attaches the decoded claims to req.auth before calling next(). Routes mounted behind it can trust req.auth.sub as the caller's id. Roles are checked separately — authentication answers 'who are you', authorization answers 'may you do this'. On the client, a 401 means the token is missing or stale: clear it and redirect to login instead of retrying forever.

examples.title: Bearer-token middleware
examples.walkthrough: Verification failure never reaches the handler. requireRole runs second, so only authenticated employers may create jobs; the client treats any 401 as 'session over'.

content.useCase: Write endpoints, user profiles, and anything scoped to the logged-in identity.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does requireAuth attach to the request?
options: The verified token payload, e.g. req.auth.sub
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Downstream handlers read the caller's id and role from the decoded claims.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should the client respond to a 401 from the API?
options: Retry the request in a loop
Clear the token and redirect to login
Ignore it and render empty data
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 401 means the session is gone or expired; retrying cannot fix it.

content.summary: Verify tokens in middleware, separate authentication from role checks, and treat 401 as an expired session.

lessons.title: Deployment and Hardening
objectives: Configure production environment variables
Apply baseline hardening and a health check

content.introduction: The gap between 'works locally' and 'safe in production' is mostly configuration: secrets, headers, limits, and a way to know when things break.
content.explanation: Production needs real secrets that never ship in the bundle, a build of the React app served as static files by (or alongside) the API, and browser security headers from helmet. Rate-limit the auth endpoints, because password guessing is a volume attack. A /health endpoint gives your platform something to poll and tells you the process is alive even when traffic is zero. Finally, watch for unhandled promise rejections — in modern Node they terminate the process, so log them deliberately.

examples.title: Baseline production setup
examples.walkthrough: helmet sets secure response headers, the limiter caps login attempts to 20 per 15 minutes, the built React bundle is served statically, and /health reports liveness for uptime checks.

content.useCase: Any deploy target: a VM, a container, or a PaaS where a platform probe hits /health.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why rate-limit the login endpoint?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Brute force depends on volume; a cap makes it impractical.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of a /health endpoint?
options: It lets a platform probe confirm the process is alive
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Orchestrators and uptime monitors poll it to decide whether to route traffic or restart the service.

content.summary: Real secrets, secure headers, rate-limited auth, a static client build, and a health check you can monitor.
